claim: Plant viruses account for enormous agricultural losses worldwide.
source: Plant viruses account for enormous agricultural losses worldwide, and the most effective way to combat them is to identify genetic material conferring plant resistance to these pathogens.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on agricultural impacts of plant viruses

claim: The most effective way to combat plant viruses is to identify genetic material conferring plant resistance to these pathogens.
source: Plant viruses account for enormous agricultural losses worldwide, and the most effective way to combat them is to identify genetic material conferring plant resistance to these pathogens.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in plant pathology and breeding

claim: A strong, replicable association was detected in a 1.5 Mb region on chromosome 2 with a 10-fold increase in relative risk of systemic necrosis.
source: We detected a strong, replicable association in a 1.5 Mb region on chromosome 2 with a 10-fold increase in relative risk of systemic necrosis.
evidence: Supported by GWA analysis data presented in the manuscript

claim: The region on chromosome 2 contains several plausible causal genes.
source: The region contains several plausible causal genes as well as abundant structural variation, including an insertion of a Copia transposon into a Toll/interleukin receptor (TIR-NBS-LRR) coding for a gene involved in defense, that could be either a driver or a consequence of the disease-resistance locus.
evidence: Based on gene annotation and functional analysis

claim: The region on chromosome 2 contains abundant structural variation, including an insertion of a Copia transposon into a TIR-NBS-LRR gene involved in defense.
source: The region contains several plausible causal genes as well as abundant structural variation, including an insertion of a Copia transposon into a Toll/interleukin receptor (TIR-NBS-LRR) coding for a gene involved in defense, that could be either a driver or a consequence of the disease-resistance locus.
evidence: Supported by structural variation analysis from long-read sequencing data

claim: Loss-of-function mutant plants of AT2G14080 exhibited different symptoms than wild-type plants when inoculated with TuMV.
source: When inoculated with TuMV, loss-of-function mutant plants of this gene exhibited different symptoms than wild-type plants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from T-DNA knockout mutants

claim: The direction and severity of symptom differences in AT2G14080 mutants depended on the adaptation history of the virus.
source: The direction and severity of symptom differences depended on the adaptation history of the virus.
evidence: Supported by comparison of mutant responses to ancestral vs. evolved virus isolates

claim: The increase in symptom severity in AT2G14080 mutants was specific for infections with the adapted isolate.
source: This increase in symptom severity was specific for infections with the adapted isolate.
evidence: Supported by experimental comparison of responses to different viral isolates

claim: Necrosis-associated alleles are found worldwide.
source: Necrosis-associated alleles are found worldwide, and their distribution is consistent with a trade-off between resistance during viral outbreaks and a cost of resistance otherwise, leading to negative frequency-dependent selection.
evidence: Supported by geographic distribution analysis of alleles

claim: The distribution of necrosis-associated alleles is consistent with a trade-off between resistance during viral outbreaks and a cost of resistance otherwise, leading to negative frequency-dependent selection.
source: Necrosis-associated alleles are found worldwide, and their distribution is consistent with a trade-off between resistance during viral outbreaks and a cost of resistance otherwise, leading to negative frequency-dependent selection.
evidence: Based on inference from geographic distribution patterns and evolutionary theory

claim: The genetic architecture of plant responses to viral infections has received much less attention than the response to bacterial and fungal pathogens.
source: In spite of this, the genetic architecture of plant responses to viral infections has received much less attention than the response to bacterial and fungal pathogens (Bartoli and Roux, 2017; Monnot et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to review literature

claim: In agricultural settings, plants are predominantly grown as monocultures, which results in more virulent and specialized viruses that cause more detrimental effects on the host.

claim: Through their specialization in one host species, viruses evolve better counter defenses than their naïve counterparts.

claim: Potyviruses affect a wide variety of crops, especially from the families Brassicaceae and Solanaceae.
source: Potyviruses affect a wide variety of crops, especially from the families Brassicaceae and Solanaceae, and are among the most widespread crop pathogens worldwide (Revers and García, 2015).

claim: Potyviruses are among the most widespread crop pathogens worldwide.
source: Potyviruses affect a wide variety of crops, especially from the families Brassicaceae and Solanaceae, and are among the most widespread crop pathogens worldwide (Revers and García, 2015).

claim: TuMV is among the most damaging of the potyviruses.

claim: TuMV has a high incidence in wild populations of A. thaliana.
source: TuMV is among the most damaging of the potyviruses (Tomlinson, 1987), and also has a high incidence in wild populations of A. thaliana (Pagán et al., 2010).

claim: The extensive genetic resources available in A. thaliana make it a useful system for investigating mechanisms of viral resistance in plants.

claim: A. thaliana belongs to the same family (Brassicaceae) as agriculturally important crops such as cauliflower, cabbage, turnip, or rapeseed.
source: In addition, A. thaliana belongs to the same family (Brassicaceae) as agriculturally important crops such as cauliflower, cabbage, turnip, or rapeseed; thus, a large array of relevant crop viruses can infect and be studied in A. thaliana (Pagán et al., 2010; Ouibrahim and Caranta, 2013).

claim: A large array of relevant crop viruses can infect and be studied in A. thaliana.
source: In addition, A. thaliana belongs to the same family (Brassicaceae) as agriculturally important crops such as cauliflower, cabbage, turnip, or rapeseed; thus, a large array of relevant crop viruses can infect and be studied in A. thaliana (Pagán et al., 2010; Ouibrahim and Caranta, 2013).

claim: Viral outbreaks are frequent in natural populations of A. thaliana.
source: Viral outbreaks are frequent in natural populations of A. thaliana, and there is substantial genetic variation in resistance, indicating that viral coevolution represents a meaningful selection pressure in this species (Pagán et al., 2010).

claim: The evolved isolate had been submitted to 12 serial passages of experimental evolution on A. thaliana Col-0 line.

claim: The two virus isolates differ in two non-synonymous mutations fixed during their adaptation to Col-0.
source: The two virus isolates differ in two non-synonymous mutations fixed during their adaptation to Col-0 and in their infection phenotypes.

claim: The two virus isolates differ in their infection phenotypes.

claim: The evolved virus has mutations in amino acids T1293I (cylindrical inclusion protein; CI) and N2039H (viral genome-linked protein; VPg).

source: CI is involved in viral genome replication and cell-to-cell movement (Deng et al., 2015), and has been shown to interact with the photosystem I PSI-K protein in A. thaliana (Jiménez et al., 2006).

claim: 1050 lines of A. thaliana were inoculated with the ancestral or evolved isolates of TuMV.
source: We inoculated 1050 lines of A. thaliana (Alonso-Blanco et al., 2016) with the ancestral (Chen et al., 2003) or evolved (González et al., 2019) isolates of TuMV and characterized the response to each one based on four phenotypes
evidence: Supported by experimental design description

claim: Four phenotypes were measured: infectivity, AUDPS, severity of symptoms, and necrosis.
source: We inoculated 1050 lines of A. thaliana (Alonso-Blanco et al., 2016) with the ancestral (Chen et al., 2003) or evolved (González et al., 2019) isolates of TuMV and characterized the response to each one based on four phenotypes: (i) infectivity (proportion of plants showing symptoms), (ii) AUDPS (area under the disease progress stairs), a measure of disease progress (Simko and Piepho, 2012), (iii) severity of symptoms on a semi-quantitative scale from 0 to 5 (Figure 1A; Butković et al., 2020), and (iv) necrosis (a binary trait reflecting presence/absence of systemic necrosis, or stage 5 of the severity-of-symptoms scale).
evidence: Supported by experimental design description

claim: Infectivity is defined as the proportion of plants showing symptoms.
source: (i) infectivity (proportion of plants showing symptoms)
evidence: Definition provided in the methods

claim: AUDPS is a measure of disease progress.
source: (ii) AUDPS (area under the disease progress stairs), a measure of disease progress (Simko and Piepho, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to the method

claim: Severity of symptoms was measured on a semi-quantitative scale from 0 to 5.
source: (iii) severity of symptoms on a semi-quantitative scale from 0 to 5 (Figure 1A; Butković et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by figure and citation to previous use of the scale

claim: Necrosis is a binary trait reflecting presence/absence of systemic necrosis, or stage 5 of the severity-of-symptoms scale.
source: (iv) necrosis (a binary trait reflecting presence/absence of systemic necrosis, or stage 5 of the severity-of-symptoms scale)

claim: Viral accumulation is significantly correlated with the intensity of symptoms within the Col-0 line.
source: We did not measure viral accumulation, but note this is significantly correlated with the intensity of symptoms within the Col-0 line (Corrêa et al. 2020), although it is not clear if this correlation occurs in all lines.

claim: There are strong correlations between AUDPS and infectivity.
